claims.text: Increasing the reducing-agent concentration increases the reduction rate.
Increasing the reaction temperature can be used as an alternative way to increase the reduction rate.
Faster reduction accelerates the simultaneous nucleation of all metal species.
Faster reduction minimizes kinetic differences arising from reduction potentials and precursor mobilities among the metal species.
Nearly simultaneous nucleation reduces phase separation and promotes atomic-level alloy homogeneity.
A kinetically controlled growth regime can govern the structure formed by noble-metal-based multimetallic nanoparticles.
Increasing atom deposition relative to surface diffusion can change nanoparticle growth mode and produce dendritic solid-solution PdPtRhIrRu nanocrystals.
Fast reduction produces a narrower particle-size distribution than slow reduction.
A homogeneous high-entropy alloy structure supports the formation of isolated noble-metal active sites.
Isolated Pt and Pd active sites can form in PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Isolated noble-metal active sites optimize substrate adsorption and enhance catalytic turnover.
Charge transfer from transition metals to Pt and Pd modulates their electronic structure, promotes nitrobenzene adsorption, and enhances nitrobenzene hydrogenation activity.
Relative to slow reduction, fast reduction will improve elemental homogeneity.
Relative to slow reduction, fast reduction will reduce particle-size dispersion.
Relative to slow reduction, fast reduction will increase catalytic turnover frequency or nitrobenzene hydrogenation yield.
The proposed relationship applies only when precursor composition is held constant and nucleation and growth kinetics dominate formation.
